- **Algorithm (exact step-by-step procedure)** [`algorithm_concept`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/algorithm_concept.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Euclid's procedure for the greatest common measure and Eratosthenes' sieve exist in Greek. Reckoning is taught as hand practice on the board, not as written rules.
- **Binary numbers** [`binary_numbers`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/binary_numbers.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept low. Needs place value first. Looks like a philosopher's game; Roman money and weights run in twelfths.
- **Boolean logic (algebra of true and false)** [`boolean_logic`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/boolean_logic.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Stoic logic (Chrysippus) already treats 'and', 'or' and 'if' between whole statements, and Cicero knows it. Turning it into calculation with symbols is new. Local: Cicero and the Stoic teachers in Roman households.
- **Switching circuits and logic gates** [`logic_gates_switching`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/logic_gates_switching.md) — K0, use none, make impossible, accept low
- **Mechanical calculator** [`mechanical_calculator`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/mechanical_calculator.md) — K2, use none, make very-hard, accept medium. Geared planetary models exist and Cicero describes them. Teeth are filed by hand as small triangles. An adding machine with a carry is new and presupposes place-value numbers. Local: Archimedes' geared sphere, booty of Marcellus from Syracuse (212 BC), kept in his family's house (Cicero, De re publica I); whether it survives in 46 BC is not recorded. Elsewhere: Rhodes: Posidonius' planetary sphere (Cicero heard him there on his journey of 79–77 BC); Greek workshops that built the device lost off Antikythera c. 70-60 BC (at least 30 bronze gears).
- **Punched cards for control and data** [`punched_card_control`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/punched_card_control.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low. Roman looms are upright and plain; figured silks arrive from the East as finished luxury cloth. There is no drawloom to control.

Books are copied by slaves from dictation and Cicero complains of faulty Latin copies. Counting lines (stichometry) is the only check; check sums need place-value arithmetic. Local: Atticus' trained copyists.

Ctesibius' float valve keeps a water clock's inflow steady; such clocks are rare luxuries in Rome. The general idea of a self-correcting machine has not been drawn. Elsewhere: Alexandria: Ctesibius' tradition of water clocks and pneumatic devices.
- **Cryptography and codebreaking (ciphers, frequency analysis, one-time pad)** [`cryptography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/cryptography.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Caesar writes confidential letters with the alphabet shifted three places. Nobody counts letter frequencies. A breaker or a better cipher interests him and his enemies. Local: Caesar; Lucius Cornelius Balbus and Gaius Oppius, who run his affairs in Rome.
